title: Points of controversy
hook: a book of debates with other early schools, set out question and answer

segments.voice: Yesterday, strong support: weather, food, people and places leaning hard on the mind. Your line: good supports.

Is the person known as a real and ultimate fact? Yes. Then is the person known in the same way as other real and ultimate facts? No, that can't be said. Then your first answer needs another look. That's roughly how one book of the Abhidhamma begins: not with a list, but with an argument. Two voices, back and forth, about whether there is a person beyond the parts. It reads less like a lecture than a transcript of a very patient debate club.
screen: `IS THE PERSON REAL?` → `YES. THEN IN THE SAME WAY?` → `A BOOK THAT ARGUES.`

segments.voice: The book is the Kathavatthu, usually translated points of controversy. It's one of the books of the Theravada Abhidhamma, and tradition says the elder Moggaliputta Tissa, whom you met at the third council on day eight hundred sixty, set it out to answer views held by other early Buddhist schools. Each debate starts with a question to the other side. The other side answers. Then the questioner follows the answer to its consequences, step by step, until a tension shows: if you say this, you must also say that, and you've already said you won't. The other side gets to push back, and in places it cites the Buddha's own words. The book doesn't name the schools it debates; the later commentary does that work. The first debate is about the person. One group of early Buddhists, known as the personalists, held that there is a person who is neither the same as body and mind nor separate from them, and they pointed to places where the Buddha speaks of a person. The Kathavatthu's side answers that such talk is a way of speaking, true in its place, but not one more ultimate thing beside matter and mind. Both sides were Buddhists, reading the same teacher closely and arriving at different answers. The book goes on through many more questions: whether an awakened person can fall back, whether past and future things exist. What's worth keeping isn't who won. It's the form. Write the other side's answer down in its own words. Follow it honestly. Let them reply.
screen: `QUESTION, ANSWER, CONSEQUENCE.` · `THE OTHER SIDE CITES THE BUDDHA TOO.` · `THE FIRST DEBATE: THE PERSON.` · then, large: `BOTH SIDES, READING ONE TEACHER.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a view you disagree with, small or big, and let it speak quietly in its own words, the way someone who holds it would say it at its best. Notice what in you wants to interrupt, let that settle, and hear the point out to its end. You don't have to agree.
Kathavatthu. Points of controversy: a book of the Abhidhamma set out as question and answer with other early schools, beginning with the person. Today's word.
Your line: points of controversy. Two sides, one teacher, and each answer heard in its own words. Day one thousand ninety.

howItsDone: Theravada scholars study the Kathavatthu as part of the Abhidhamma, with its commentary naming the schools behind each view, and monastic debate and question-and-answer study continue in several Buddhist traditions.

chat.says: Did early Buddhists ever disagree with each other about the teaching?
options: Yes: the Kathavatthu records debates with other early schools, both sides citing the Buddha.
No: every early Buddhist held exactly the same views, and splits came only centuries later.
Yes, but the book only lists the other views, with no replies and no quotes from the Buddha.
chat.meaning: The Kathavatthu sets out question-and-answer debates with other early schools. Both sides were Buddhists, reading the same teacher and reaching different answers.

notes: The hook's opening exchange paraphrases the start of Kathavatthu I.1 (Shwe Zan Aung and C. A. F. Rhys Davids' Points of Controversy renders it with 'the soul'/'person'); not quoted. Confirm the paraphrase.
'The first debate is about the person' (Kathavatthu I.1); a claim that it is also the longest was cut under the claims rule.
Moggaliputta Tissa's authorship is given as 'tradition says'; the third council setting and Ashoka are left out under the claims rule.
The personalists (Pudgalavada: Vatsiputriya, Sammitiya) described as holding a person neither identical to nor different from the aggregates; confirm the framing is fair to them.
'In places it cites the Buddha's own words': the opponent cites sutta passages speaking of a person (e.g. the person who works for his own welfare). Confirm.
Topics named: falling back of an arahant (I.2) and whether past and future exist (I.6, the 'all exists' debate); confirm.
